Green’s Functions

Purdue University
Course-material provenance

This page was migrated from the CHM 696 course materials developed by Jonathan Hood and Lyudmila Slipchenko. Equations and examples remain under editorial review during the Fall 2026 website migration.

Learning goals¶

By the end of this lecture, you should be able to:

  • interpret a Green’s function as an inverse-operator kernel and impulse response;

  • distinguish boundary-condition and retarded Green’s functions;

  • construct the retarded Green’s function of a damped oscillator; and

  • derive a spectral representation from eigenvalues and eigenfunctions.

Delta Function¶

  • The Dirac delta function δ(x)\delta(x)δ(x) is a generalized function or distribution.

  • The Dirac delta function is commonly used in physics and engineering to represent idealized point sources or impulses.

  • When integrating over it and another function f(t)f(t)f(t), it "picks out" the value of the function at a specific point:

∫abf(t) δ(t−t0) dt=f(t0)for a<t0<b\int_a^b f(t) \, \delta(t - t_0) \, dt = f(t_0) \quad \text{for } a < t_0 < b∫ab​f(t)δ(t−t0​)dt=f(t0​)for a<t0​<b
(1)

This property indicates that the delta function evaluates a function f(t)f(t)f(t) at t=t0t = t_0t=t0​, and outside this interval, the integral is zero.

  • The delta function is normalized as follows:

∫−∞∞δ(x) dx=1\int_{-\infty}^{\infty} \delta(x) \, dx = 1∫−∞∞​δ(x)dx=1
(2)

Delta Function (continued)¶

  • While the delta function is not a proper function, it can be viewed as the limit of a family of normalized functions.

  • One common representation is in terms of a top-hat functions:

Πa(x)={1aif ∣x∣<a20otherwise\Pi_a(x) = \begin{cases} \frac{1}{a} & \text{if } |x| < \frac{a}{2} \\ 0 & \text{otherwise} \end{cases}Πa​(x)={a1​0​if ∣x∣<2a​otherwise​
(3)

  • Another common representation is in terms of a Gaussian. In the limit as a→0a \to 0a→0:

δa(x)=1∣a∣πe−x2/a2\delta_a(x) = \frac{1}{|a|\sqrt{\pi}} e^{-x^2/a^2}δa​(x)=∣a∣π​1​e−x2/a2
(4)

This approximation is useful in numerical analysis, where δ(x)\delta(x)δ(x) can be represented and manipulated as a limit of smooth functions.

  • Both of these functions satisfy the normalization condition:

∫−∞∞δa(x) dx=1\int_{-\infty}^{\infty} \delta_a(x) \, dx = 1∫−∞∞​δa​(x)dx=1
(5)

  • As a→0a \to 0a→0, these functions converge to the delta function: δ(x)=lim⁡a→0δa(x)\delta(x) = \lim_{a \to 0} \delta_a(x)δ(x)=lima→0​δa​(x)

Properties of the delta function¶

For a smooth test function ϕ\phiϕ,

∫ϕ(x)δ(x−x0) dx=ϕ(x0),∫ϕ(x)δ′(x−x0) dx=−ϕ′(x0).\int\phi(x)\delta(x-x_0)\,dx=\phi(x_0), \qquad \int\phi(x)\delta'(x-x_0)\,dx=-\phi'(x_0).∫ϕ(x)δ(x−x0​)dx=ϕ(x0​),∫ϕ(x)δ′(x−x0​)dx=−ϕ′(x0​).
(6)

Useful scaling and composition identities include

δ(ax)=1∣a∣δ(x),δ(g(x))=∑xi:g(xi)=0δ(x−xi)∣g′(xi)∣,\delta(ax)=\frac{1}{|a|}\delta(x), \qquad \delta(g(x)) =\sum_{x_i:g(x_i)=0}\frac{\delta(x-x_i)}{|g'(x_i)|},δ(ax)=∣a∣1​δ(x),δ(g(x))=xi​:g(xi​)=0∑​∣g′(xi​)∣δ(x−xi​)​,
(7)

when the zeros xix_ixi​ are simple.

Green’s functions: Introduction¶

  • The Green’s function provides a powerful method for solving inhomogeneous linear equation systems.

  • The Green’s function generalizes the concept of an inverse matrix or an impulse response to continuous systems.

  • The Green’s function is fundamentally defined as the response of the linear system to a unit impulse.

  • Let’s write the linear equation system as Ly(x)=f(x)Ly(x)=f(x)Ly(x)=f(x), where f(x)f(x)f(x) represents the forcing term or input.

  • The Green’s function uses the same linear differential operator and the boundary or initial conditions chosen for the original problem:

LG(x,z)=δ(x−z)L G(x, z) = \delta(x-z)LG(x,z)=δ(x−z)
(8)

  • Away from the source point x=zx=zx=z, it satisfies the corresponding homogeneous equation.

  • Physically, G(x,z)G(x,z)G(x,z) may be thought of as the response of the system at position xxx resulting from a unit-strength point source located at position zzz.

Green’s functions: Introduction (continued)¶

  • If the boundary conditions are built into GGG, the solution is

y(x)=∫abG(x,z)f(z)dzy(x) = \int_{a}^{b} G(x, z) f(z) dzy(x)=∫ab​G(x,z)f(z)dz
(9)

  • This integral means that the response of the system to a distributed force f(x)f(x)f(x) is the superposition of the individual responses (GGG) to infinitesimal impulses comprising f(x)f(x)f(x).

  • For a time-translation-invariant system, G(t,t′)=g(t−t′)G(t,t')=g(t-t')G(t,t′)=g(t−t′) and the integral is a convolution. For a general operator, G(x,z)G(x,z)G(x,z) depends on its two arguments separately and the integral is not necessarily a convolution.

  • In case of the linear differential operator LLL, the solution is formally y=L−1fy=L^{-1}fy=L−1f. The Green’s function G(x,z)G(x,z)G(x,z) is the kernel that defines this inverse linear operator L−1L^{-1}L−1 through integration.

Driving force¶

  • Let’s consider an inhomogeneous linear equation:

Dy(t)=f(t)D y(t) = f(t)Dy(t)=f(t)
(10)

DDD is a linear operator that represents any linear ordinary differential equation (ODE).

  • f(t)f(t)f(t) represents some driving force acting on the system. We can view it as a sum of delta functions:

f(t)=∑iciδ(t−ti)f(t) = \sum_i c_i \delta(t - t_i)f(t)=i∑​ci​δ(t−ti​)
(11)

  • In continuous form, this becomes

f(t)=∫0∞f(t′)δ(t′−t) dt′f(t) = \int_0^\infty f(t') \delta(t' - t) \, dt'f(t)=∫0∞​f(t′)δ(t′−t)dt′
(12)

  • This representation implies that f(t)f(t)f(t) can be thought of as a sum of "kicks" applied to the system at different times. If we find the response of the system to one of these kicks, then we can just sum up all of these responses for each kick to get the total response. This is the idea of the Green’s function.

What the original figure plots. It shows hand-drawn decomposition of a driving function into impulses and their shifted responses.

What this is trying to convey. Impulse decomposition and superposed responses from Jonathan’s original Green’s-function notes.

Polished version.

Green’s function definition¶

  • Next, we define the Green’s function as the solution to the ODE with a delta function as the source term.

  • The Green’s function G(t,t′)G(t, t')G(t,t′) satisfies:

Dy(t)=f(t)D y(t) = f(t)Dy(t)=f(t)
(13)
DG(t,t′)=δ(t−t′)D G(t, t') = \delta(t - t')DG(t,t′)=δ(t−t′)
(14)
y(t)=∫0∞GR(t,t′)f(t′) dt′,y(t) = \int_0^\infty G_{\mathrm{R}}(t, t') f(t') \, dt',y(t)=∫0∞​GR​(t,t′)f(t′)dt′,
(15)

  • The Green’s function G(t,t′)G(t, t')G(t,t′) represents the system’s response to a delta function "kick" applied at time t′t't′.

  • The retarded Green’s function obeys GR(t,t′)=0G_{\mathrm{R}}(t,t')=0GR​(t,t′)=0 for t<t′t<t't<t′, so the fixed-domain integral receives contributions only from earlier source times. It becomes an ordinary convolution when the coefficients are time-translation invariant.

Proof for the Green’s function¶

  • Using a fixed integration domain avoids extra boundary terms from a time-dependent upper limit:

Dy(t)=Dt(∫0∞GR(t,t′)f(t′) dt′)D y(t) =D_t\left(\int_0^\infty G_{\mathrm{R}}(t,t')f(t')\,dt'\right)Dy(t)=Dt​(∫0∞​GR​(t,t′)f(t′)dt′)
(16)

  • Since DDD is a linear operator that operates on ttt, it can be applied inside the integral:

Dy(t)=∫0∞[DtGR(t,t′)]f(t′) dt′D y(t) =\int_0^\infty \bigl[D_tG_{\mathrm{R}}(t,t')\bigr]f(t')\,dt'Dy(t)=∫0∞​[Dt​GR​(t,t′)]f(t′)dt′
(17)

  • By definition, the Green’s function G(t,t′)G(t, t')G(t,t′) satisfies the following equation:

DtGR(t,t′)=δ(t−t′)D_t G_{\mathrm{R}}(t, t') = \delta(t - t')Dt​GR​(t,t′)=δ(t−t′)
(18)

  • Substituting this back into the expression for Dy(t)D y(t)Dy(t):

Dy(t)=∫0∞δ(t−t′)f(t′) dt′=f(t).D y(t) =\int_0^\infty\delta(t-t')f(t')\,dt' =f(t).Dy(t)=∫0∞​δ(t−t′)f(t′)dt′=f(t).
(19)

Proof for the Green’s function (continued)¶

This verifies the differential equation provided the interchange of the operator and integral is justified and the Green’s function enforces the required initial or boundary conditions.

Example: Driven damped harmonic oscillator¶

  • Consider the driven damped harmonic oscillator:

y′′(t)+2γy′(t)+ω02y(t)=f(t)y''(t) + 2\gamma y'(t) + \omega_0^2 y(t) = f(t)y′′(t)+2γy′(t)+ω02​y(t)=f(t)
(20)

where γ\gammaγ is the damping coefficient and ω0\omega_0ω0​ is the natural frequency of the undamped system.

  • We start by defining the Green’s function G(t,t′)G(t, t')G(t,t′) for this system, which satisfies:

G′′(t,t′)+2γG′(t,t′)+ω02G(t,t′)=δ(t−t′)G''(t, t') + 2\gamma G'(t, t') + \omega_0^2 G(t, t') = \delta(t - t')G′′(t,t′)+2γG′(t,t′)+ω02​G(t,t′)=δ(t−t′)
(21)

with retarded support GR(t,t′)=0G_{\mathrm{R}}(t,t')=0GR​(t,t′)=0 for t<t′t<t't<t′. Integrating across t=t′t=t't=t′ shows that GRG_{\mathrm{R}}GR​ is continuous and its first derivative has the unit jump

∂tGR(t′+,t′)−∂tGR(t′−,t′)=1.\partial_tG_{\mathrm{R}}(t'^+,t') -\partial_tG_{\mathrm{R}}(t'^-,t')=1.∂t​GR​(t′+,t′)−∂t​GR​(t′−,t′)=1.
(22)

  • To find G(t,t′)G(t, t')G(t,t′), we take the Laplace transform of both sides. Let L{G(t,t′)}=G~(p,t′)\mathcal{L}\{G(t, t')\} = \tilde{G}(p, t')L{G(t,t′)}=G~(p,t′), where ppp is the Laplace variable.

  • The Laplace transform of the differential equation yields:

p2G~(p,t′)−pG(0,t′)−∂tG(0,t′)+2γ ⁣[pG~(p,t′)−G(0,t′)]+ω02G~(p,t′)=L{δ(t−t′)}.p^2 \widetilde G(p,t')-pG(0,t')-\partial_tG(0,t') +2\gamma\!\left[p\widetilde G(p,t')-G(0,t')\right] +\omega_0^2\widetilde G(p,t') =\mathcal{L}\{\delta(t-t')\}.p2G(p,t′)−pG(0,t′)−∂t​G(0,t′)+2γ[pG(p,t′)−G(0,t′)]+ω02​G(p,t′)=L{δ(t−t′)}.
(23)

Example: Driven damped harmonic oscillator (continued)¶

  • The Laplace transform of the differential equation yields:

p2G~(p,t′)−pG(0,t′)−∂tG(0,t′)+2γ ⁣[pG~(p,t′)−G(0,t′)]+ω02G~(p,t′)=L{δ(t−t′)}.p^2 \widetilde G(p,t')-pG(0,t')-\partial_tG(0,t') +2\gamma\!\left[p\widetilde G(p,t')-G(0,t')\right] +\omega_0^2\widetilde G(p,t') =\mathcal{L}\{\delta(t-t')\}.p2G(p,t′)−pG(0,t′)−∂t​G(0,t′)+2γ[pG(p,t′)−G(0,t′)]+ω02​G(p,t′)=L{δ(t−t′)}.
(24)

  • Given the initial conditions G(0,t′)=0G(0, t') = 0G(0,t′)=0 and G′(0,t′)=0G'(0, t') = 0G′(0,t′)=0, this simplifies to:

(p2+2γp+ω02)G~(p,t′)=e−pt′(p^2 + 2\gamma p + \omega_0^2) \tilde{G}(p, t') = e^{-p t'}(p2+2γp+ω02​)G~(p,t′)=e−pt′
(25)

  • Thus:

G~(p,t′)=e−pt′p2+2γp+ω02\tilde{G}(p, t') = \frac{e^{-p t'}}{p^2 + 2\gamma p + \omega_0^2}G~(p,t′)=p2+2γp+ω02​e−pt′​
(26)

  • We now take the inverse Laplace transform to find G(t,t′)G(t, t')G(t,t′):

GR(t,t′)=Θ(t−t′) e−γ(t−t′)ωdsin⁡ ⁣[ωd(t−t′)],G_{\mathrm{R}}(t,t') =\Theta(t-t')\,\frac{e^{-\gamma(t-t')}}{\omega_d} \sin\!\left[\omega_d(t-t')\right],GR​(t,t′)=Θ(t−t′)ωd​e−γ(t−t′)​sin[ωd​(t−t′)],
(27)

where ωd=ω02−γ2\omega_d=\sqrt{\omega_0^2-\gamma^2}ωd​=ω02​−γ2​. This form assumes the underdamped case γ<ω0\gamma<\omega_0γ<ω0​; critical and overdamped systems have the corresponding repeated-root or hyperbolic-sine limits.

  • This Green’s function represents the system’s response to an impulsive force applied at time t′t't′.

Example: Driven damped harmonic oscillator (continued)¶

  • Using the Green’s function, the general solution to the original equation is given by:

y(t)=∫0∞GR(t,t′)f(t′) dt′y(t) = \int_0^\infty G_{\mathrm{R}}(t,t')f(t')\,dt'y(t)=∫0∞​GR​(t,t′)f(t′)dt′
(28)

  • Substituting the expression for G(t,t′)G(t, t')G(t,t′):

y(t)=1ωd∫0te−γ(t−t′)sin⁡[ωd(t−t′)]f(t′) dt′.y(t) = \frac{1}{\omega_d}\int_0^t e^{-\gamma(t-t')}\sin[\omega_d(t-t')]f(t')\,dt'.y(t)=ωd​1​∫0t​e−γ(t−t′)sin[ωd​(t−t′)]f(t′)dt′.
(29)

  • This solution shows that the system’s response at time ttt is a sum of the responses to the source term f(t′)f(t')f(t′) at all previous times t′t't′, weighted by the Green’s function. The Green’s function incorporates both the damping and the oscillatory nature of the harmonic oscillator.

System of linear equations¶

  • Let’s try to solve matrix equation

(EI−H)a=b,(E\mathbf{I} - \mathbf{H})\mathbf{a} = \mathbf{b},(EI−H)a=b,
(30)

where EEE is a scalar, H\mathbf{H}H is an N×NN\times NN×N Hermitian matrix, and a,b\mathbf{a},\mathbf{b}a,b are vectors. The inverse exists only when EEE is not an eigenvalue of H\mathbf{H}H.

  • The standard approach is to find inverse of (EI−H)(E\mathbf{I} - \mathbf{H})(EI−H):

G(E)=(EI−H)−1\mathbf{G}(E) = (E\mathbf{I} - \mathbf{H})^{-1}G(E)=(EI−H)−1
(31)

  • If G(E)\mathbf{G}(E)G(E) is found, the original equation can be solved for any b\mathbf{b}b:

a=(EI−H)−1b=G(E)b\mathbf{a} = (E\mathbf{I} - \mathbf{H})^{-1}\mathbf{b} = \mathbf{G}(E)\mathbf{b}a=(EI−H)−1b=G(E)b
(32)

System of linear equations (continued)¶

  • For a diagonalizable matrix,

Aqi=λiqi  →  A−1=QΛ−1Q−1,\mathbf{A}\mathbf{q}_i = \lambda_i \mathbf{q}_i \; \rightarrow \; \mathbf{A}^{-1} = \mathbf{Q}\Lambda^{-1} \mathbf{Q}^{-1},Aqi​=λi​qi​→A−1=QΛ−1Q−1,
(33)

where Q\mathbf{Q}Q is the matrix of eigenvectors and Λ\LambdaΛ is the diagonal matrix of eigenvalues. For a Hermitian matrix, Q−1=Q†\mathbf{Q}^{-1}=\mathbf{Q}^\daggerQ−1=Q†.

  • Then if HCα=EαCα,\mathbf{H}\mathbf{C}^{\alpha} = E_{\alpha}\mathbf{C}^{\alpha},HCα=Eα​Cα, α=1,2,…,N\alpha=1,2,\dots,Nα=1,2,…,N:

(G(E))ij=∑αCiαCjα∗E−Eα(\mathbf{G}(E))_{ij} = \sum _{\alpha} \frac{C_i^{\alpha}C_j^{\alpha*}}{E-E_{\alpha}}(G(E))ij​=α∑​E−Eα​Ciα​Cjα∗​​
(34)

  • Elements of G(E)\mathbf{G}(E)G(E) "blow up" (have poles) when E is equal to eigenvalues of H\mathbf{H}H.

  • G(E)\mathbf{G}(E)G(E) is a Green’s function associated with H\mathbf{H}H.

Inhomogeneous differential equation¶

  • Now consider inhomogeneous differential equation:

(E−H^)a(x)=b(x),(E-\hat{H})a(x) = b(x),(E−H^)a(x)=b(x),
(35)

where E - parameter, H^\hat{H}H^ - Hermitian differential operator.
We solve for a(x)a(x)a(x).

  • Assume for simplicity that H^\hat HH^ has a complete discrete orthonormal eigenbasis:

H^ψα(x)=Eαψα(x)\hat{H} \psi_\alpha (x) = E_{\alpha} \psi_{\alpha}(x)H^ψα​(x)=Eα​ψα​(x)
(36)

  • Expand a(x)a(x)a(x) and b(x)b(x)b(x) into eigenstates of H^\hat{H}H^:

a(x)=∑αaαψα(x)a(x) = \sum_{\alpha} a_{\alpha} \psi_{\alpha}(x)a(x)=α∑​aα​ψα​(x)
(37)
b(x)=∑αbαψα(x)b(x) = \sum_{\alpha} b_{\alpha} \psi_{\alpha}(x)b(x)=α∑​bα​ψα​(x)
(38)

Here, we can compute bα=∫dx′ψα∗(x′)b(x′)b_\alpha= \int dx' \psi_\alpha ^*(x') b(x')bα​=∫dx′ψα∗​(x′)b(x′).
However, we do not know aαa_\alphaaα​ - these need to be determined.

Inhomogeneous differential equation (continued)¶

  • Plug in a(x)a(x)a(x) and b(x)b(x)b(x) into the original equation:

∑αaα(E−H^)ψα(x)=∑αbαψα(x)\sum_\alpha a_{\alpha}(E-\hat{H})\psi_{\alpha}(x) = \sum_{\alpha} b_{\alpha} \psi_{\alpha}(x)α∑​aα​(E−H^)ψα​(x)=α∑​bα​ψα​(x)
(39)

  • Since ψα\psi_\alphaψα​ are eigenstates of H^\hat{H}H^:

∑αaα(E−Eα)ψα(x)=∑αbαψα(x)\sum_\alpha a_{\alpha}(E-E_\alpha)\psi_{\alpha}(x) = \sum_{\alpha} b_{\alpha} \psi_{\alpha}(x)α∑​aα​(E−Eα​)ψα​(x)=α∑​bα​ψα​(x)
(40)

  • Multiplying from left by ψα∗(x)\psi_\alpha^*(x)ψα∗​(x), integrating and using orthogonality of eigenstates ψα\psi_\alphaψα​:

aα(E−Eα)=bαa_{\alpha}(E-E_\alpha) = b_{\alpha}aα​(E−Eα​)=bα​
(41)

  • Solution:

a(x)=∑αbαE−Eαψα(x)=∫dx′[∑αψα(x)ψα∗(x′)E−Eα]b(x′)a(x) = \sum_{\alpha} \frac{ b_{\alpha}}{E-E_\alpha}\psi_\alpha(x)= \int dx' \Bigl[ \sum_\alpha \frac{\psi_\alpha(x)\psi_\alpha^*(x')}{E-E_\alpha} \Bigr] b(x')a(x)=α∑​E−Eα​bα​​ψα​(x)=∫dx′[α∑​E−Eα​ψα​(x)ψα∗​(x′)​]b(x′)
(42)

Inhomogeneous differential equation (continued)¶

a(x)=∑αbαE−Eαψα(x)=∫dx′[∑αψα(x)ψα∗(x′)E−Eα]b(x′)a(x) = \sum_{\alpha} \frac{ b_{\alpha}}{E-E_\alpha}\psi_\alpha(x)= \int dx' \Bigl[ \sum_\alpha \frac{\psi_\alpha(x)\psi_\alpha^*(x')}{E-E_\alpha} \Bigr] b(x')a(x)=α∑​E−Eα​bα​​ψα​(x)=∫dx′[α∑​E−Eα​ψα​(x)ψα∗​(x′)​]b(x′)
(43)

  • Green’s function G(x,x′,E)G(x,x',E)G(x,x′,E):

G(x,x′,E)=∑αψα(x)ψα∗(x′)E−EαG(x,x',E) = \sum_\alpha \frac{\psi_\alpha(x)\psi_\alpha^*(x')}{E-E_\alpha}G(x,x′,E)=α∑​E−Eα​ψα​(x)ψα∗​(x′)​
(44)

  • Then solution can be written as:

a(x)=∫dx′G(x,x′,E)b(x′)a(x) = \int dx' G(x,x',E) b(x')a(x)=∫dx′G(x,x′,E)b(x′)
(45)

  • Similarly to matrix equation, solution to the differential equation with any input (driving force) is known as long as its Green’s function is found.

  • The resolvent has poles at isolated discrete eigenvalues. At such an energy the inverse is undefined unless a prescription such as E→E±i0E\to E\pm i0E→E±i0 or a projection away from the null space is specified. Continuous spectra require integrals in addition to the discrete sum.

Inhomogeneous differential equation (continued)¶

  • Suppose b(x)=δ(x−x′)b(x)=\delta(x-x')b(x)=δ(x−x′).

  • Then:

a(x)=∫dz G(x,z;E)δ(z−x′)=G(x,x′;E).a(x)=\int dz\,G(x,z;E)\delta(z-x')=G(x,x';E).a(x)=∫dzG(x,z;E)δ(z−x′)=G(x,x′;E).
(46)

  • Substituting in the original differential equation:

(E−H^)G(x,x′,E)=δ(x−x′)(E-\hat{H})G(x,x',E) = \delta(x-x')(E−H^)G(x,x′,E)=δ(x−x′)
(47)

  • This is differential equation for G(x,x′,E)G(x,x',E)G(x,x′,E).

  • In matrix form:

(EI−H)(EI−H)−1=I.(E\mathbf{I} - \mathbf{H})(E\mathbf{I} - \mathbf{H})^{-1} = \mathbf{I}.(EI−H)(EI−H)−1=I.
(48)

Homework for this lecture¶

Existing final-project option¶

In this problem, you will derive the Green’s function for the time-dependent Schrödinger equation for a free particle in one dimension.

The time-dependent Schrödinger equation for a free particle is given by:

iℏ∂ψ(x,t)∂t=−ℏ22m∂2ψ(x,t)∂x2i \hbar \frac{\partial \psi(x,t)}{\partial t} = - \frac{\hbar^2}{2m} \frac{\partial^2 \psi(x,t)}{\partial x^2}iℏ∂t∂ψ(x,t)​=−2mℏ2​∂x2∂2ψ(x,t)​
(49)

where ψ(x,t)\psi(x,t)ψ(x,t) is the wavefunction.

We are now going to define the Green’s function for this problem. Note that this is a PDE now position and time. We are going to define the Green’s function as the solution for a wavefunction localized at a position x′x'x′ at t=0t=0t=0, ψ(x,t=0)=δ(x−x′)\psi(x,t=0) = \delta(x-x')ψ(x,t=0)=δ(x−x′). The Green’s function is the resulting solutions. Therefore, the Green’s function G(x,x′,t)G(x, x', t)G(x,x′,t) solves the equation:

iℏ∂G(x,x′,t)∂t=−ℏ22m∂2G(x,x′,t)∂x2i \hbar \frac{\partial G(x, x', t)}{\partial t} = - \frac{\hbar^2}{2m} \frac{\partial^2 G(x, x', t)}{\partial x^2}iℏ∂t∂G(x,x′,t)​=−2mℏ2​∂x2∂2G(x,x′,t)​
(50)

with the initial condition:

G(x,x′,0)=δ(x−x′).G(x, x', 0) = \delta(x - x').G(x,x′,0)=δ(x−x′).
(51)

The equation for the wavefunction ψ(x,t)\psi(x,t)ψ(x,t) in terms of the Green’s function G(x,x′,t)G(x, x', t)G(x,x′,t) and the initial wavefunction ψ(x′,0)\psi(x', 0)ψ(x′,0) is given by the convolution of the Green’s function with the initial condition. This is:

ψ(x,t)=∫−∞∞G(x,x′,t)ψ(x′,0) dx′\psi(x,t) = \int_{-\infty}^{\infty} G(x, x', t) \psi(x', 0) \, dx'ψ(x,t)=∫−∞∞​G(x,x′,t)ψ(x′,0)dx′
(52)

where: ψ(x,t)\psi(x, t)ψ(x,t) is the wavefunction at position xxx and time ttt, G(x,x′,t)G(x, x', t)G(x,x′,t) is the Green’s function, which represents the evolution of the wavefunction from x′x'x′ at time 0 to xxx at time ttt, and ψ(x′,0)\psi(x', 0)ψ(x′,0) is the initial wavefunction at t=0t = 0t=0. The integral runs over all possible initial positions x′x'x′, accounting for the contribution of each part of the initial wavefunction to the final state.

This equation represents the time evolution of an arbitrary initial state ψ(x′,0)\psi(x', 0)ψ(x′,0) under the free particle Schrödinger equation, using the Green’s function to propagate the state forward in time.

Step 1¶

To solve this equation, start by taking the Fourier transform of the Green’s function with respect to x−x′x - x'x−x′. Define the Fourier transform as:

G~(k,t)=∫−∞∞G(x,x′,t)e−ik(x−x′) dx\tilde{G}(k,t) = \int_{-\infty}^{\infty} G(x, x', t) e^{-ik(x - x')} \, dxG~(k,t)=∫−∞∞​G(x,x′,t)e−ik(x−x′)dx
(53)

where kkk is the wavenumber.

Step 2¶

You should be left with a first order ODE in time. Solve this first order ODE. Hint: You should get

G~(k,t)=exp⁡(−iℏk22mt)\tilde{G}(k,t) = \exp\left(-i \frac{\hbar k^2}{2m} t\right)G~(k,t)=exp(−i2mℏk2​t)
(54)

Initial Condition in Fourier Space¶

Now use the initial condition G(x,x′,0)=δ(x−x′)G(x, x', 0) = \delta(x - x')G(x,x′,0)=δ(x−x′) to determine G~(k,0)\tilde{G}(k, 0)G~(k,0). Hint: The Fourier transform of the delta function δ(x−x′)\delta(x - x')δ(x−x′) is 1. Therefore, G~(k,0)=1\tilde{G}(k, 0) = 1G~(k,0)=1.

Inverse Fourier Transform¶

Now you have the solution of the Green’s function in the Fourier domain. Now, take the inverse Fourier transform to return to position space:

G(x,x′,t)=12π∫−∞∞G~(k,t)eik(x−x′) dkG(x, x', t) = \frac{1}{2\pi} \int_{-\infty}^{\infty} \tilde{G}(k,t) e^{ik(x - x')} \, dkG(x,x′,t)=2π1​∫−∞∞​G~(k,t)eik(x−x′)dk
(55)

Hint: This is a Gaussian integral. You can use the standard result for integrals of the form:

∫−∞∞exp⁡(−Ak2+Bk) dk=πAexp⁡(B24A)\int_{-\infty}^{\infty} \exp(-A k^2 + B k) \, dk = \sqrt{\frac{\pi}{A}} \exp\left(\frac{B^2}{4A}\right)∫−∞∞​exp(−Ak2+Bk)dk=Aπ​​exp(4AB2​)
(56)

with appropriate constants AAA and BBB.

Solve the Integral¶

The Green’s function for the time-dependent Schrödinger equation is:

G(x,x′,t)=m2πiℏtexp⁡(im(x−x′)22ℏt)G(x, x', t) = \sqrt{\frac{m}{2\pi i \hbar t}} \exp\left( i \frac{m (x - x')^2}{2 \hbar t} \right)G(x,x′,t)=2πiℏtm​​exp(i2ℏtm(x−x′)2​)
(57)

This Green’s function represents the probability amplitude for a particle to propagate from position x′x'x′ at time t=0t = 0t=0 to position xxx at time ttt.

Propagate solutions¶

Plot the solution ∣ψ(x,t)∣2|\psi(x,t)|^2∣ψ(x,t)∣2 at various times for ψ(x,t=0)=δ(x)\psi(x,t=0) = \delta(x)ψ(x,t=0)=δ(x). Hint it diverges for t=0t=0t=0 so start a little later. The goal is for you to understand what is going on. Plot whatever you want.
